candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Moral truth requires a mind-grounded, nonarbitrary source, while atheism cannot justify universally binding moral values from consequences alone.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening argument is delivered by Matt after Scott explicitly asks him to present his case from the ground up.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Matt's foundational route from truth and moral value to a transcendent source and directly challenges the secular alternative in the motion.
candidates.contextSummary: Matt develops an initial account of truth as mind-dependent, asks how moral statements obtain truth value, and argues that secular consequential assignments become arbitrary and cannot impose universal obligations.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Secular moral inquiry can begin with the substantive aim of improving well-being, while definitions themselves need not function as truth claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott takes the floor after Matt yields and explicitly contrasts top-down and bottom-up approaches while explaining his own practical moral concern.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presents a secular alternative to Matt's proposed foundation and answers the charge that defining morality through welfare is an arbitrary truth claim.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's claim that secular welfare-based morality lacks truth value and becomes arbitrary.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott distinguishes conceptual analysis from a bottom-up inquiry focused on happiness, flourishing, and avoidable suffering, then argues that a moral definition is not itself the proposition requiring truth evaluation.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Morality is grounded in God's immutable character rather than arbitrary divine commands, and goodness is known through God's self-revelation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt expressly rejects the divine-command formulation attributed to him and states the character-based Christian account during the ensuing exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal pro-side specification of how God grounds morality and is essential to distinguishing Matt's view from arbitrary command theory.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Scott's formulation that moral and immoral acts are respectively commanded or forbidden by God.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt rejects arbitrary command theory, identifies God's nature and essence as the moral standard, and says humans discover goodness because the eternal divine character is revealed to them.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Defining goodness by God's actual attributes leaves no independent basis for judging those attributes good and therefore makes morality arbitrary or accidental.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott leads the questioning throughout this passage, identifies the absence of an external standard, and develops the dishonest-God counterfactual in his own turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presses the central arbitrariness objection against a divine-nature theory even after arbitrary divine-command theory has been disclaimed.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's claim that God's immutable character is the standard of goodness disclosed through revelation.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott argues that calling honesty good merely reports that God happens to be honest, then asks whether God controls his character and whether a divine nature of dishonesty is genuinely impossible.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Appealing only to God's fixed identity does not explain why a contrary divine nature is impossible, so the divine standard remains modally unexplained.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott repeatedly advances and refines the possible-world and hypothetical-world challenge, with Matt's short answers serving as the objects of that sustained examination.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This develops the arbitrariness objection into a modal challenge about whether God's moral character has any reason or necessity beyond bare identity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's answer that God cannot lie because dishonesty conflicts with God's revealed, unchanging nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott distinguishes God's inability to change from the possibility of an eternally different nature, challenges identity-based answers as circular, and constructs a world where opposite divine traits set opposite moral standards.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: A counterfactual that reverses God's essential character cannot adjudicate divine morality because it abandons the very theological principles under examination.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt directly answers the proposed alternate divine nature, explains why he will not grant it, and concludes by restating his revealed-character account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Matt's principal response to the modal arbitrariness challenge and defends the necessity of the divine nature underlying his moral foundation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Scott's hypothetical world in which God's immutable traits are dishonest and hateful rather than honest and loving.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt declines to reason from a scenario that contradicts God's holiness, distinguishes a truth-related thought experiment from redefining God, and grounds objective morals in God's actual righteous character and revelation.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: If God is the sole standard used to evaluate God, believers cannot noncircularly determine whether that standard is good rather than profoundly harmful.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott clarifies the counterfactual, tests dishonesty for logical impossibility, and then explicitly states the circular-standard objection as the conclusion of his questioning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly disputes whether God can provide a rationally evaluable necessary foundation for morality rather than merely a self-certifying standard.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's insistence that God's actual immutable holiness and internal logical consistency exclude a dishonest divine nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott separates an eternally different nature from a change in nature, argues that lying is not logically impossible in itself, and concludes that Matt lacks a standard independent of God for recognizing divine goodness.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: A divine-nature account supplies no rational reason to obey God because its justification that God is good collapses back into conformity with God's nature.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott supplies the extended practical example and carries it through the successive questions about wrongness, divine nature, goodness, and reasons for compliance.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This converts the circularity critique into a challenge about normative authority, addressing whether a divine foundation can generate reasons and obligations for agents.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's position that humans lack the standing or sufficient knowledge to judge God's morality.

candidates.contextSummary: Using a disputed sexual prohibition, Scott traces the proposed justification from wrongness to God's nature and then to God's goodness, arguing that the circular definitions leave the commanded person without a rational reason to comply.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: God's omniscience distinguishes divine moral revelation from human judgment because God knows every actual and potential consequence relevant to action.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt responds immediately to Scott's practical objection and explicitly invokes divine omniscience to distinguish God from an ordinary human adviser.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response offers an epistemic basis for divine moral authority and introduces complete knowledge of consequences as an answer to the comparison with human standards.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Scott's claim that God's nature is unevaluable and therefore provides no rational basis for obedience.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt says Scott's reasoning leads toward moral agnosticism, contrasts limited human knowledge with God's knowledge of all actual and possible facts, and argues that divine prescriptions may rest on reasons humans cannot fully understand.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: If omniscience makes God morally authoritative by supplying otherwise unavailable facts, then access to those facts could remove the need for God as the standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: Scott explicitly identifies Matt's invocation of omniscience, frames its relevance as a new question, and reaches the stated implication at the final owned-core row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move tests whether the proposed divine foundation is genuinely constitutive of morality or merely an informational substitute for facts humans presently lack.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt's claim that God's exhaustive knowledge gives divine revelation moral authority unavailable to ordinary humans.

candidates.contextSummary: Scott asks why omniscience makes God a better moral standard than an ordinary person and whether God functions only as a source of facts which, if independently known, would make divine authority unnecessary.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: God's omniscience makes divine moral guidance relevant because God knows every consequence and can therefore make perfect judgments about actions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly answers Clifton's question about omniscience and consistently presents Slick's divine-knowledge argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This connects divine omniscience to practical moral judgment and answers the objection that unavailable facts would make God dispensable as a moral authority.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that complete factual knowledge, rather than God, would suffice for moral judgment.

candidates.contextSummary: After Clifton asks why omniscience makes God a better moral standard, Slick argues that Clifton already evaluates actions by their ends and that God uniquely knows all ends.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: If consequences determine which actions are right, omniscience makes God an informational intermediary rather than the foundation that makes those actions right.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly develops a hypothetical theistic concession and draws the intermediary-versus-standard distinction in his own turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction directly contests whether God grounds morality or merely communicates independently grounded moral facts about consequences.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's argument that God's exhaustive knowledge of consequences explains divine moral authority.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton grants for argument that humans might defer to an omniscient being, then argues that consequences would remain the truth-makers while God only transmits information.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: God's immutable nature and self-glorifying will constitute the Christian moral standard, while finite subjective agents cannot coherently judge God by an external standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: The extended uninterrupted turn states the Christian account in first-person apologetic terms and contrasts divine attributes with human subjectivity.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Slick's core grounding thesis and his central objection to secular evaluation: only God's nature is objective, whereas human standards remain finite and subjective.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's distinction between God as a source of information and the independent basis of moral rightness.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick clarifies that morality reflects God's nature and purposes, then argues that non-omniscient created agents possess no objective vantage point from which to judge God.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Moral standards can resemble conventional measurement standards: the chosen definition may be arbitrary while judgments made against it remain objectively true or false.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces and develops the ruler analogy immediately after Slick's objection to subjective standards.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy challenges the inference from objective judgments to a divinely existing standard by separating conventional definitions from objective application.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's contention that a subjective standard cannot yield knowledge of moral truth or judge an objective God.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton compares morality with defining a foot by a ruler, arguing that no transcendent ruler is required for propositions to be objectively assessed once a standard is fixed.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Because moral absolutes require an objective standard and secular alternatives cannot justify one, eliminating the atheistic option validates the theistic account.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick identifies his eliminative argumentative form and explicitly contrasts atheistic and theistic justification of moral absolutes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a direct formulation of the pro side's transcendental or impossibility-to-the-contrary case for God as the necessary basis of objective morality.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's effort to characterize Slick's position as an inference to the best explanation and question its structure.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick says ubiquitous moral absolutes demand an objective standard, claims competing atheistic standards are arbitrary, and concludes that negating atheism leaves theism validated.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: The universal wrongness of torturing babies for pleasure is justified by God's revealed prohibition of murder and therefore exemplifies a divinely grounded moral absolute.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick defines moral absolutes, supplies the torture example, and expressly grounds its truth in divine revelation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The concrete example is offered as the test case that secular morality must justify and as evidence that divine revelation supplies an objective standard.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's request for the ontology and meaning of the moral absolutes Slick claims require explanation.

candidates.contextSummary: After being pressed to identify what moral absolutes are, Slick defines them as universally true principles independent of humans and grounds a paradigmatic prohibition in revelation.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: The claim that rape is wrong can express the objectively assessable proposition that rape causes unnecessary suffering, even if the moral definition itself is selected by humans.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly identifies the truth claim he means by moral wrongness and distinguishes observable suffering from the choice of moral terminology.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This presents a secular route to objective moral truth by grounding evaluation in mind-independent facts about suffering rather than in divine commands or nature.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's claim that Clifton can assert actions are wrong but cannot justify those assertions without an external divine standard.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton explains that suffering is empirically real and assessable independently of his opinion, while acknowledging that Slick may instead challenge his chosen definition of morality.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: A secret assault on an unconscious person would remain wrong despite producing no awareness, disease, pregnancy, or discovered harm, exposing an insufficiency in harm-based morality.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick constructs the coma scenario and expressly applies it as a counterexample to Clifton's stated harm criterion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The thought experiment directly tests whether secular harm reduction can explain a firm moral judgment in a case stipulated to lack the harms Clifton emphasized.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's account of rape's wrongness as an objectively verifiable instance of unnecessary suffering and harm.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick stipulates an undiscovered assault whose unconscious victim experiences no identified consequences, then asks whether Clifton's criterion must classify the act as not wrong.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: A secular moral account can consider actual and potential conscious states and rule-level social consequences, rather than simply maximizing immediate aggregate happiness.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton refines his definition and uses the organ-harvesting thought experiment to explain broader consequences of adopting a rule.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The refinement answers a central counterexample by showing how secular moral reasoning can incorporate potential states, expectations, security, and institutional rules.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's assertion that the unconscious-victim scenario makes Clifton's harm-based definition inconsistent.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton broadens the relevant domain to actual and potential conscious states, then argues against harvesting one person's organs by considering the fearful society that permission would create.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Contractarian reasoning behind a veil of ignorance can generate impartial rules for social conduct without requiring God because the rational construction is hypothetical.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces a named secular approach and fully explains the rational-choice and veil-of-ignorance mechanism across the boundary lookahead.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This gives an affirmative secular foundation for moral rules, directly addressing the motion by explaining how impartial obligations can be reasoned out without divine existence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's repeated demand for a secular justification of wrongness that is neither arbitrary nor dependent on God.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton asks the parties to imagine perfectly rational rule-makers who do not know their own identities or interests, so their negotiated rules avoid bias and require no deity.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: A secular preference-based account makes the moral status of an action vary with recipients' preferences and therefore cannot supply an objective standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and Slick's explicit second-person criticism clearly attribute this sustained objection to Matt Slick.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly attacks Clifton's proposed secular foundation by arguing that its dependence on preferences produces incompatible moral verdicts for the same action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's contractualist and harm-oriented explanation of why an unobserved rape remains morally wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: After Clifton introduces a veil-of-ignorance contractual model, Slick argues that preference-sensitive judgments make identical conduct good or bad depending on the recipient.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: A divine moral theory is circular because God can be evaluated as the moral standard only by appealing back to God himself.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly contrasts his nuanced moral system with Slick's system and states the circularity objection in his own turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges the explanatory adequacy of the proposed divine foundation and tests it with the possibility of a God who desires universal misery.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's demand for a concise secular moral standard and his claim that God's revealed character supplies one.

candidates.contextSummary: Responding to Slick's request for a compact standard, Clifton says moral inquiry is necessarily more complex and argues that defining God through God is circular.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Secular moral definitions are arbitrary because they rest in personal choice, whereas moral truth rests in God's revealed character rather than human intuition.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick expressly contrasts morality grounded in God's character with morality grounded in Clifton's character and cites divine revelation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states Slick's principal grounding distinction between divine revelation and human preference, directly supporting the pro side's answer to the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that moral intuitions can be evaluated against the meanings assigned to right and wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of intuition and arbitrariness, Slick maintains that revealed prohibitions allow moral knowledge without recursively validating one's own intuitions.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Divine-command morality can in principle separate right and wrong entirely from suffering, happiness, health, and other real-world consequences.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces the objection as a problem with Slick's worldview and develops the universal-misery hypothetical directly.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument contests whether God's nature supplies a substantively credible moral foundation by showing that it could label maximal misery moral by definition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's assertion that conduct such as homosexual relationships is wrong whenever God declares it wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: After Slick treats divine declaration as decisive, Clifton argues that this account can disregard welfare entirely and again invokes a universal-misery counterexample.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Atheism cannot justify a non-subjective objective moral standard, while Christian obligation follows from God's nature, human creation for his glory, and eventual judgment.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick resumes his lost train of thought, addresses Clifton by name, and delivers an extended first-person defense of the Christian position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a direct affirmative case for the motion, combining a transcendental objection to secular morality with a practical illustration of allegedly unanswerable moral wrongdoing.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's request for a reason to adopt Slick's worldview and his statement that threatened consequences may not motivate him.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick argues that secular appeals to harm or social agreement are unjustified preferences and illustrates the claimed result with a coercive theft scenario.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Even complete acceptance of Christianity's factual and moral claims does not by itself provide a motivating reason that compels someone to obey them.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly sets up and repeatedly clarifies a role-playing counterexample in which he accepts every proposition in Slick's worldview.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The thought experiment targets the gap between identifying an act as divinely prohibited and supplying an action-guiding reason, exposing a central normative challenge to theism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's claim that accepting his Christian worldview would prevent a person from committing grave wrongdoing.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton imagines accepting Christianity while intending to molest a baby, then argues that beliefs about God, punishment, and wrongness remain descriptions or prescriptions he can disregard.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Christians may knowingly violate moral requirements, but inconsistency between belief and practice does not undermine the existence of objective moral truth.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick introduces the revised scenario, cites his counseling experience, and explicitly distinguishes Christian profession from inconsistent practice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This answers Clifton's motivational counterexample by separating moral ontology from compliance and restates the charge that atheism lacks an objective standard.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's scenario in which someone accepts every Christian proposition yet still intends to commit an atrocity.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick concedes that believers can act against acknowledged duties, treats this as inconsistency rather than disproof, and renews his challenge to atheistic condemnation.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: An action can possess inherent moral rightness or wrongness only if an absolute God identifies it as consistent or inconsistent with his nature.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick explicitly frames the issue as moral ontology and contrasts an absolute divine nature with an atheistic worldview.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The proposition gives the pro side's direct metaphysical answer to the debate by claiming that intrinsic moral properties require an absolute divine foundation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that consequences, rather than God, are the relevant standard for evaluating morality.

candidates.contextSummary: During clarification about consequences, Slick distinguishes consequences after an act from the act's moral essence and argues atheistic definitions remain intuitive and arbitrary.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Moral status is not intrinsic to actions but arises from their real-world consequences together with agents' intentions and related circumstances.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly identifies this as a major difference between their views and states his own account in direct contrast to Slick's.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the con side's affirmative alternative to intrinsic divine morality by locating moral evaluation in consequences, intentions, and contextual features.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's contention that actions have an ontological moral essence grounded only in an absolute God's nature.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton crystallizes the disagreement by denying inherent moral status and offering a consequence-and-intention account as the secular basis for evaluating conduct.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Defining right as what ought to be done does not establish that God's commands are right, because no reason has been supplied for the claimed obligation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton conditionally accepts Slick's definition of right and then directly disputes the unsupported identification of divine commands with obligation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This exposes a purported inferential gap between divine commands and normative authority, challenging whether the proposed foundation actually yields duties for agents.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's assertion that one ought to follow what is right simply because right means what ought to be followed.

candidates.contextSummary: At the core boundary, Clifton accepts the definitional link between rightness and obligation but denies that Slick has connected God's commands to that category.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Facts about divine creation and ownership cannot by themselves yield prescriptions about how a person ought to act.
candidates.attributionBasis: The row begins with the end of Slick's sentence, but Clifton's objection starts distinctly with the reference to facts and continues through the prescription claim.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly challenges the proposed inference from God's status as creator and owner to binding moral obligations, a central foundation of the pro case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's claim that God's creation and ownership give him the right to prescribe human conduct.

candidates.contextSummary: After Slick invokes divine creation and ownership as grounds for authority, Clifton identifies those claims as descriptions and denies that prescriptions follow from them.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Christianity can bridge the is-ought gap because its descriptions and prescriptions coincide, whereas an atheistic system cannot derive the ought.
candidates.attributionBasis: The wording expressly defends the prior prescription, invokes the Christian worldview, and contrasts it with Clifton's atheistic system in Slick's argumentative voice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The claimed ability of the Christian worldview uniquely to ground obligations is a direct argument that objective moral prescriptions require a divine foundation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's objection that facts about God remain descriptions from which no moral prescription can be derived.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick answers the is-ought objection by asserting that Christianity unifies description and prescription and by charging arbitrary atheism with an unbridgeable gap.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Claims that God created humanity, is powerful, defines morality, or can punish people remain descriptions that do not explain why anyone should obey God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker introduces a list of Slick's divine claims as examples and explicitly applies Clifton's recurring descriptive-versus-prescriptive objection to them.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The examples concretize the central secular rebuttal that adding divine attributes and sanctions does not logically establish a binding reason for moral obedience.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's assertion that Christian description and prescription are the same and therefore bridge the is-ought gap.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton tests Slick's proposed bridge with several facts about God and argues that none of them supplies the missing normative reason to follow divine commands.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: People ought to do what is right because doing so glorifies God, the supreme object of worship and the proper moral standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: The response explicitly reiterates what Slick says he has already told Clifton and invokes God's glory, worship-worthiness, and status as the moral standard.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Slick's direct positive account of why divine consistency generates obligation, placing God's normative supremacy at the foundation of morality.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that divine attributes and powers do not provide a reason why anyone ought to obey God's commands.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick responds that right conduct is required because it accords with and glorifies God, whom he identifies as both the highest object of worship and the right standard.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: The theistic inference to the best explanation fails against someone who denies that the alleged phenomenon of moral absolutes exists at all.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator expressly gives Clifton the first closing statement, and Clifton identifies Matt's moral argument before denying the phenomenon it purports to explain.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This closing argument attacks the explanatory starting point of the pro case: absent the purported moral absolutes, their alleged need for a divine explanation is moot.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's inference that God is the best or necessary explanation for the existence of objective moral absolutes.

candidates.contextSummary: In his closing statement, Clifton distinguishes approaches to moral inquiry and argues that his worldview incurs no explanatory deficit by rejecting Slick's posited absolutes.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: A secular moral system can perform the practical work Slick demands because neither worldview can guarantee that its condemnation will stop a determined wrongdoer.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly summarizes what he has tried to argue and compares his worldview with Matt's by revisiting their shared inability to stop a rapist through argument alone.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The parity claim answers a recurring practical challenge to secular morality and supports Clifton's broader contention that theism offers no unique functional advantage.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's challenge that secular morality cannot objectively condemn or effectively restrain someone intent on rape.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton evaluates moral systems by what they accomplish and argues that both sides stand on equal footing regarding incentives or the ability to deter wrongdoing.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: Defining goodness through God's nature is circular because God must be evaluated by the same standard he constitutes, rendering the resulting moral claims vacuous.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly labels Matt's definition circular, reconstructs the God-and-goodness relation, and states the alleged consequence for theistic moral claims.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges whether the proposed divine standard is coherently objective at all, directly contesting the pro side's foundational identification of goodness with God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's definition of moral rightness as consistency with God's essentially good nature and character.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton argues that Slick cannot independently assess God's fitness as a moral standard because the proposed evaluative standard is identical with the object being evaluated.

candidates.speaker: Scott Clifton
candidates.proposition: The charge that secular morality is arbitrary also applies to theistic morality, while Christianity still fails to derive prescriptions from descriptions about God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Clifton expressly attributes the arbitrariness criticism to Matt, applies it back to Matt's definition, and restates the failure to obtain a prescription from Christianity.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move combines a parity rebuttal with the is-ought objection, undermining two claimed comparative advantages of the divine-foundation account at once.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Slick's contention that Clifton's secular moral standard is arbitrary whereas God's nature supplies a nonarbitrary obligation.

candidates.contextSummary: Clifton says Slick merely refers to conformity with God's nature without justifying obedience, leaving the Christian account subject to arbitrariness and the same normative gap.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Some initial circularity is unavoidable and not disqualifying, while judging God by an external standard would contradict the very conception of God under dispute.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator has handed the closing statement to Slick, who concedes circularity on both sides and directly answers Clifton's demand for a standard by which to judge God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Slick's principal defense of the divine standard against Clifton's circularity objection and explains why no norm external to God is admissible within his account.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's argument that Slick cannot establish God's goodness because evaluating God by God's own standard is circular.

candidates.contextSummary: Slick accepts that both worldviews begin with presuppositions, denies that this alone invalidates either, and argues that an external standard would negate his concept of God.

candidates.speaker: Matt Slick
candidates.proposition: Clifton's proposed moral standard remains arbitrary, whereas an objective standard can be found in God through biblical revelation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Slick directly addresses Clifton's claimed objectivity, calls the secular account arbitrary, then positively identifies the Bible as the means of finding his own objective standard.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states the pro side's comparative conclusion and source of moral knowledge, contrasting an allegedly arbitrary secular criterion with revealed divine objectivity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Clifton's claim that his secular account avoids arbitrariness while the God-based account lacks independent justification.

candidates.contextSummary: Continuing his closing response, Slick disputes the objectivity of Clifton's standard and appeals to biblical revelation as access to the objective divine moral standard.
